name: Mbelime
confidence_why: Liu 2013, Kombetto et al. 2017 and Neukom 2004/2005 all describe Mbelime as a three-level tone language (high, mid, low, with contrastive minimal pairs) and none gives a word-stress rule; Neukom's passing remarks on an undefined 'accent' on the first syllable of disyllabic verbs and on the stative verb in compounds add detail without contesting the tonal classification.
catalog_citation: Liu, Rachel. 2013. Tone in Mbelime nouns. Série électronique de documents de travail (SIL Togo-Bénin) 1: 1-45. Lomé: SIL Togo-Bénin. Open-access SIL PDF (46 pp.).
catalog_locator: §1 Introduction, p. 3, paragraph beginning 'The three underlying tone levels in Mbelime'; §3.3 'H melody on disyllabic noun roots', p. 8, paragraph following example (10) 'si pibi-si'.
catalog_quote: The three underlying tone levels in Mbelime are high, mid and low. These underlying tone levels combine to form six underlying tone melodies on noun roots, which I will refer to by their surface representations: L, M, H, S (super high), ML, and LH. The precise natures of the melodies I refer to as H and S in underlying form are not yet clear, and are subjects in need of further study. Important tonal processes include automatic downstep, high tone raising, and low tone spreading. [p. 3] ... This alternation may have something to do with stress or phonological phrasing, as well as probable tonelessness of epenthetic vowels (recall that in simple CVCV noun stems, the second vowel is epenthetic). Mbelime speakers only recognize the difference in pronunciation when it is repeatedly pointed out to them. [p. 8]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated by any accessible source. Mbelime is described first-hand (Liu 2013; Melick 2012) as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus a surface super-high) with upstep, automatic downstep and low-tone spread; the only mention of stress is Liu's speculation that a surface-tone alternation on CVCV noun roots might reflect stress or phrasing. Corroborated second-hand by Roberts, Boyd, Merz & Vydrin 2020: 116 ('three contrastive level tones, H, M and L, contour tones, downstep, upstep').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Liu's remark concerns isolation vs phrase-medial realisations of noun tone melodies (citation forms vs phrase); Melick's data are verb forms in frames. Neither addresses a word-stress domain.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language (mbel1240, ISO mql, spoken around Cobly, Atacora, Benin). Liu 2013's consultant is from Kountori (living in Cobly); Neukom 2004 was based on four weeks with one speaker from Namounchaga (fieldwork in Kara, Togo); no dialect split is drawn by any source.

new_statements.quote: Comme la plupart des langues africaines, le mbèlimè est une langue tonale. Le ton d'un mot s'écrit selon sa mélodie telle qu'elle se prononce. Le mbèlimè a trois tons distinctifs : le ton haut, le ton moyen et le ton bas. Le ton s'indique sur toutes les voyelles. On emploie l'accent aigu ( ́ ) pour marquer le ton haut et l'accent grave ( ̀ ) pour marquer le ton bas. On ne marque rien pour le ton moyen.
new_statements.translation: Like most African languages, Mbelime is a tone language. The tone of a word is written according to its melody as it is pronounced. Mbelime has three distinctive tones: high, mid and low. Tone is marked on all vowels. The acute accent is used to mark high tone and the grave accent to mark low tone. Nothing is marked for mid tone.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Liu 2013 statement (tone language, no stress statement) and with the empty catalog rule: three tone levels, no word-stress rule given.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orthography guide only: Mbelime is a three-level tone language (H, M, L) with contour tones on short vowels and tonal processes (lowering of H suffixes, L on verbs after ù/bɛ̀/past dɛ, a floating M as an assertive marker). The word 'accent' occurs only as the name of the diacritics (accent aigu, accent grave); nothing is said about word stress or prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; tonal notes: H suffixes -sí, -í, -ú, -mú are sometimes heard lowered (p. 13); imperfective verbs take L tones after ù, bɛ̀ or past dɛ (p. 14)
new_statements.identity_note: No work names a dialect. Kombetto et al. 2017 is the standard orthography of the Commission Nationale Linguistique Mbèlimè for the Bèbèlibè of the Cobly and Boukombé communes (Atacora, Benin). Neukom's grammar rests on one informant during a four-week stay in Togo/Benin plus SIL manuscripts (Hammond, Hamilton, Rietkerk, Bättig), with recorded texts; he flags parts of his verb-tone data as insecure.

new_statements.quote: Le perfectif ne porte jamais de ton modulé. Les verbes dissyllabiques manifestent un choix en ce qui concerne la deuxième position: a) soit qu'il porte un ton moyen ou haut et porte l'accent, ce qui résulte en les schèmes tonals B–M ou M–H (la structure syllabique est CVCV́), b) soit qu'il porte un ton bas (l'accent reste sur la première syllabe). || (i) L'accent du substantif composé tombe sur le verbe statif; c'est pourquoi le radical substantival apparaît sous sa forme réduite, c'est-à-dire sa voyelle est brève et monophtongue || Au plan phonologique le mbèlimè distingue trois tons ponctuels, haut (H), moyen (M) et bas (B).
new_statements.translation: The perfective never carries a contour tone. Disyllabic verbs show a choice for the second position: a) either it carries a mid or high tone and carries the accent, which results in the tone patterns L–M or M–H (the syllable structure is CVCV́), b) or it carries a low tone (the accent stays on the first syllable). || (i) The accent of the compound noun falls on the stative verb; this is why the noun root appears in its reduced form, i.e. its vowel is short and a monophthong || At the phonological level Mbelime distinguishes three level tones, high (H), mid (M) and low (L).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the tone-only catalog entry and with Liu 2013's remark that a surface-tone alternation 'may have something to do with stress'; adds the only explicit accent statements found: default first-syllable accent in disyllabic verbs, shifted in the perfective, and accent on the verb in compounds. The catalog rule field is empty, so nothing is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Neukom describes Mbelime as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus HL and ML contours, downdrift, downstep, L- and H-spread) and has no accent section, but he uses a word accent twice in passing: in disyllabic verbs the accent is on the first syllable by default and moves to the second syllable in perfective forms whose final syllable carries M or H tone (structure CVCV́, patterns L–M / M–H); in noun + stative-verb compounds the accent falls on the verb (the second element) and the noun root reduces to a short monophthong. So accent, where mentioned, is initial in the simple verb and morphologically shifted, and it correlates with vowel length (the accented element keeps its long vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: Verb accent shifts to the final syllable in perfective forms with a non-low final tone (p. 117-118); in compounds the accent goes to the stative verb and the first member is reduced (p. 92, p. 57). Neukom warns his tone-class inventory is preliminary (fn. 16, p. 117) and that the tonal processes in compounding are under-documented (p. 56).
new_statements.identity_note: No work names a dialect. Kombetto et al. 2017 is the standard orthography of the Commission Nationale Linguistique Mbèlimè for the Bèbèlibè of the Cobly and Boukombé communes (Atacora, Benin). Neukom's grammar rests on one informant during a four-week stay in Togo/Benin plus SIL manuscripts (Hammond, Hamilton, Rietkerk, Bättig), with recorded texts; he flags parts of his verb-tone data as insecure.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another. Kombetto et al. 2017 (and the already-read Liu 2013 and Melick 2012) treat Mbelime purely as a three-level tone language and say nothing about word stress; Neukom 2004/2005 agrees on the tone system but additionally mentions a word 'accent' in two places (default first syllable of disyllabic verbs, shifting to a non-low final syllable in the perfective; accent on the stative verb in compounds, with reduction of the noun root). Neukom never defines the accent or gives it a section, so a 'tone language, no stress rule' reading remains defensible; the difference between the sources is one of silence, not of placement. Rietkerk 2000 was not opened.
